question: Do I need a cookie banner for Plausible? Our legal team also wants to know where visitor data is stored.
reference_answer: No cookies are set, so there's nothing to consent to and no cookie banner is required. All visitor data is processed and stored in the EU on servers owned and operated by European companies, and it never leaves the EU.
key_facts: No cookies are set so no cookie banner required
Data is stored and processed in the EU
answer: Plausible doesn't use cookies, doesn't store anything on your visitors' devices and doesn't collect personal data [1]. That means there's nothing for your visitors to consent to, and Plausible can run outside your cookie banner [1]. If Plausible is the only tool on your site, you may not need a consent banner at all [2]. All visitor data is processed and stored in the EU on servers owned and operated by European companies, and never leaves the EU [3].

evidence.title: Use Plausible alongside a consent management platform
evidence.text:
Plausible doesn't use cookies, doesn't store anything on your visitors' devices and doesn't collect personal data. That means there's nothing for your visitors to consent to, and Plausible can run outside your cookie banner. Your legal team may confirm that consent is not required. See our data policy and this legal assessment for the details.

Many sites still need a consent management platform (CMP) for other things they embed, such as YouTube videos, social media widgets or ad pixels. You can keep your CMP for those and let Plausible count every visitor. The goal is simple: your CMP keeps blocking the tools that need consent, but doesn't block the Plausible script.

## Check whether your CMP blocks Plausible today

Many CMPs scan your site and automatically block third-party scripts until a visitor accepts. Some treat any analytics script as a "Statistics" or "Performance" tool, including ones that don't use cookies.

To check, open your site in a private browser window and don't touch the banner. Then look at your Plausible dashboard. If your own visit shows up in the realtime view, Plausible isn't blocked and you don't need to change anything. If it doesn't, follow the steps for your CMP below. You can also use our manual verification steps.

Make sure you only exclude the Plausible script. Everything else your CMP blocks should stay blocked until visitors consent.

evidence.title: Security and compliance overview
evidence.text:
Plausible does not collect personal data or track individual users. There are no cookies, no cross-site tracking and no persistent user identifiers. Because of this, Plausible is typically classified as a low-risk service in vendor security assessments and GDPR impact analyses.

The specific reasons it falls into this category:

- No personal data is collected. Plausible does not store IP addresses, device fingerprints or any other persistent identifiers.
- No cookies are set. There is nothing to consent to and no cookie banner is required. If you run a banner for other tools, Plausible can load outside it.
- All visitor data is processed and stored in the EU on servers owned and operated by European companies, and never leaves the EU.
- No data is shared with or sold to third parties.
- A DPA is in place automatically for all customers, covering GDPR processor obligations.

question: Where can I see which pages people visit before they sign up for a trial?
reference_answer: Use user journeys in the Explore tab with an end point: begin from a conversion goal such as a trial signup and work backwards to see what path led visitors to it.
key_facts: Use the Explore tab (user journeys)
Choose the conversion goal as the end point and work backwards
answer: You can use an End point to begin from a conversion goal and work backwards [1]. Open the Explore tab from the report navigation bar, alongside Goals, Properties and Funnels [2].

citations.quote: End point: Begin from a conversion goal and work backwards.
Open the Explore tab from the report navigation bar, alongside Goals, Properties and Funnels.

evidence.title: User journeys
evidence.text:
You can explore journeys in two directions.

**Starting point:** Begin from a page or event and follow what visitors did next. Use this when you want to understand where visitors go after a key page, such as your pricing page or your post-signup confirmation screen.

**End point:** Begin from a conversion goal and work backwards. Use this when you want to understand what path led visitors to a specific outcome, such as a trial signup or a completed purchase.

evidence.title: User journeys
evidence.text:
The **Explore** tab lets you map the paths visitors actually take on your site. Pick any page, goal or event as a starting point and see what they did next. Or work backwards from a conversion to see what led visitors there.

* Works with your pages and events. No extra setup required.
* Pages from the same directory are automatically grouped to reduce noise and surface patterns more clearly
* Individual pages within a group are also selectable if you want to drill into a specific URL
* Shows "No further action" at each step so you can see how many visitors dropped off
* Displays the conversion rate for the full journey you are exploring
* All existing dashboard filters apply, so you can narrow journeys by traffic source, country, device or any other dimension

User journeys

## How to use user journeys

Open the **Explore** tab from the report navigation bar, alongside Goals, Properties and Funnels.

You'll see a list of your most visited pages and most triggered events. Select one to begin exploring the journey. Scroll down and click on "Show 10 more" to see the expanded list, or use the search bar to search for the exact page or event and set it as the starting or end point.

Each column shows the next step in the path:

* **Starting point:** the page or event you choose as the entry to the journey
* **1 step after:** what visitors did immediately after the starting point
* **2 steps after:** what visitors did after that, narrowed to those who followed the path so far

Click any item in a column to select it and load the next step. You can go up to a maximum of 20 steps. The conversion rate in the top right updates to reflect the share of starting-point visitors who reached the selected item.

To clear your selection and start over, click the **refresh icon** in the top right corner.

question: my site is a react spa. do i need extra setup to count page changes, and does going from /products to /products?page=2 count as a new pageview?
reference_answer: No extra configuration is needed, since Plausible integrates automatically with pushState-based routers like React's. A new pageview is counted when the path changes, but a query-string-only change such as /products to /products?page=2 isn't counted.
key_facts: No extra configuration for pushState routers
A pageview is counted when the path changes
Query-string-only changes are not counted
answer: If you're running a singlepage application with React, Angular, Vue or similar frameworks, you don't need to add any extra configuration to make analytics work [1]. If only the query string changes, such as going from `/products` to `/products?page=2`, it isn't counted as a new pageview [1].

citations.quote: If you're running a single-page application with React, Angular, Vue or similar frameworks, you don't need to add any extra configuration to make analytics work.
If only the query string changes, such as going from `/products` to `/products?page=2`, it isn't counted as a new pageview.

evidence.title: Single-page application support
evidence.text:
Plausible Analytics integrates automatically with modern `pushState` based frontend routers. If you're running a single-page application
with React, Angular, Vue or similar frameworks, you don't need to add any extra configuration to make analytics work.

You can verify this by installing the Plausible Analytics script and checking the **Network** tab in your devtools. Each time you navigate to a new page, an HTTP POST request to `https://plausible.io/api/event` should be triggered.

A new pageview is counted when the path changes. If only the query string changes, such as going from `/products` to `/products?page=2`, it isn't counted as a new pageview.

If you're using a frontend framework that uses the URL hash for routing, you need to take an extra step to install the hash-based tracker instead of the default one. See details here.

Note:
Using Next.js or Gatsby.js? Next.js has a bug that loads async scripts twice, causing double counting in Plausible. Gatsby.js exhibits the same behaviour. Use workarounds mentioned in the Github issue to load the Plausible script just once.

question: Is there a way to see which of my pages have poor page speed ratings according to Plausible?
reference_answer: Yes. Once Core Web Vitals tracking is set up, click the Core Web Vitals goal in the Goals section and open the Properties tab. Choose `rating` and filter for `rating` is `poor`, and the Top Pages report will show which pages those events came from.
key_facts: Filter by the Core Web Vitals goal
Add a filter for rating is poor
The Top Pages report then shows which pages need the most work
answer:
1. In the Goals section at the bottom of your dashboard, click Core Web Vitals to filter by it [1].
2. Open the Properties tab, choose metric and click LCP, INP or CLS to filter by that metric [1].
3. Choose rating to see how many page loads were good, needed improvement or were poor [1].
Add a filter for rating is poor to find the pages that need the most work [1].

evidence.title: Track Core Web Vitals with Plausible
evidence.text:
1. In the **Goals** section at the bottom of your dashboard, click **Core Web Vitals** to filter by it.
2. Open the **Properties** tab, choose `metric` and click **LCP**, **INP** or **CLS** to filter by that metric.
3. Choose `rating` to see how many page loads were good, needed improvement or were poor.

With these filters on, the **Top Pages** report shows which pages the events came from. Add a filter for `rating` is `poor` to find the pages that need the most work. More on filtering by custom properties.

These are ratings from your real visitors, not lab tests, so they reflect the devices and connections your audience actually uses. Plausible shows the share of each rating, not the timings themselves.

question: im leaving plausible at the end of the month, what happens to my sites and data if i stop paying?
reference_answer: After you cancel, you keep full access until the end of your billing period. Once it ends your dashboard is locked, though you can still log in and export your data, and after a month data collection stops. We may eventually delete your sites and stats, and we email you before that happens.
key_facts: Full access until the end of the billing period
Dashboard locks afterwards but data can be exported
Plausible emails you before deleting sites and stats
answer: Until the end of your billing period, your stats keep being counted and you have full access to your dashboard [1]. Once the billing period ends, your dashboard is locked, and while you can still log in and access your account, team and site settings, you cannot view your stats [1]. You can export your collected data at any time from the site settings of any locked site [1]. One month after locking, Plausible stops collecting data, and any data sent by the snippet will be dropped automatically from that point [1]. Once you cancel and your paid period ends, we may delete your sites and stats after emailing you first [1].

Your dashboard is locked. You can still log in and access your account, team and site settings, but you cannot view your stats.
You can export your collected data at any time from the site settings of any locked site.
One month after locking, Plausible stops collecting data. If you haven't removed the Plausible snippet from your site, any data it sends will be dropped automatically from that point.
Once you cancel and your paid period ends, we may delete your sites and stats. We'll email you before that happens so you have time to export your data or resubscribe.

evidence.title: Cancel your subscription plan
evidence.text:
Log in to your Plausible account. In the top right menu, click your account name and open the settings.

Go to the **Subscription** section and click **Cancel plan**.

Cancel your Plausible subscription

## What happens after you cancel

**Until the end of your billing period**

Your stats keep being counted and you have full access to your dashboard.

The **Subscription** section may still say **Renews on**, but your subscription ends without renewing.

**Once the billing period ends**

Your dashboard is locked. You can still log in and access your account, team and site settings, but you cannot view your stats. You can export your collected data at any time from the site settings of any locked site.

One month after locking, Plausible stops collecting data. If you haven't removed the Plausible snippet from your site, any data it sends will be dropped automatically from that point.

**Deleting your stats**

Once you cancel and your paid period ends, we may delete your sites and stats. We'll email you before that happens so you have time to export your data or resubscribe.

You can delete individual sites at any time, before or after canceling, from your site settings. To delete your entire account or team, you'll first need to cancel any active subscription.

**Resubscribing**

You can resubscribe at any time from the **Subscription** section of your settings. Your dashboards unlock automatically and data collection resumes immediately. If you subscribe again from the same account before your paid period ends, you keep your current plan and its limits.

If you resubscribe before your data is deleted, your historical stats will still be there. Deleted data cannot be recovered, so if you're coming back, resubscribe or export your data before the deletion date in our email.

Want to switch plans instead of canceling? See Change your subscription plan.

question: my api key says it can't see a client's site, i'm only a guest viewer on their site. why
reference_answer: A Stats API key is scoped to the team it was created for, so it can't query sites owned by another team or sites where you're only a Guest Viewer or Guest Editor. The client's team would need to create a key scoped to their team.
key_facts: Keys are scoped to the team they were created for
Cannot query sites where the key owner is only a Guest Viewer or Guest Editor
Client team must create the key
answer: A Stats API key can query sites owned by the team it was created for and cannot query sites where the key owner is only a Guest Viewer or Guest Editor [1].

citations.quote:
A Stats API key can query sites owned by the team it was created for. It cannot query:

- Sites owned by another team
- Sites where the key owner is only a Guest Viewer or Guest Editor

evidence.title: Plausible Stats API reference
evidence.text:
A Stats API key can query sites owned by the team it was created for. It cannot query:

- Sites owned by another team
- Sites where the key owner is only a Guest Viewer or Guest Editor

For example, suppose you are a Guest Viewer for a client's site. A Stats API key that you create under **My personal sites** cannot query that client's site. The client team would need to create a key scoped to their team.

Note:
A Stats API key can also use the read-only endpoints of the Sites API, for example to list the sites owned by its team. Creating, changing or deleting sites needs a Sites API key.

question: does the data studio connector eat up my api request limit? and how fresh is the data it shows
reference_answer: By default the connector caches data for six hours, which makes reports quicker and limits the number of API requests. Stats API keys are limited to 600 requests per hour by default. To bypass the cache and get current data, check Data Refreshed in Real-time.
key_facts: Data is cached for six hours by default
Stats API keys have a 600 requests per hour default limit
Check Data Refreshed in Real-time to bypass the cache
answer: Stats API keys are limited to 600 requests per hour by default [1]. Unless you've checked the Data Refreshed in Real-time box, the connector caches data for up to 6 hours [2].

citations.quote: Stats API keys are limited to 600 requests per hour by default.
Unless you've checked the Data Refreshed in Real-time box, the connector caches data for up to 6 hours

evidence.title: Plausible Data Studio connector
evidence.text:
You can select one or more of your Plausible sites to create a custom report. Simply tick the box next to each site that you want to include data for.

At this stage, you can check **Allow "Plausible Site(s)" to be modified in reports**. This default option in Data Studio lets you add a dropdown in your report to switch between your Plausible sites. If you don’t check it, you won’t have this feature.

Check the **Data Refreshed in Real-time** box to bypass the connector's six-hour cache and fetch current data for report queries.

If this box is not checked, the connector caches data for six hours. This makes reports quicker and limits the number of API requests. Stats API keys are limited to 600 requests per hour by default. If you need more capacity, please contact us.

Once these options are configured, you can click **Connect** and you will see a list of all available fields for data and metrics that you can pull from Plausible.

Configure the Plausible Data Studio connector

evidence.title: Plausible Data Studio connector
evidence.text:
**A report shows null values or an error.** Check your combination of dimensions and metrics. Session metrics such as Bounce Rate, Views per Visit and Visit Duration cannot be combined with event dimensions such as Goal Name or Custom Prop. If a combination returns null values or an error, use the Visitors metric instead or move the dimension into a filter. Our Data Studio guide covers these combinations with examples.

**A newly configured custom property or goal doesn't show up.** Unless you've checked the **Data Refreshed in Real-time** box, the connector caches data for up to 6 hours, so new values can take that long to appear in your report. If you need them immediately, edit the connection and enable real-time refresh. Refreshing fields only updates the data source schema, not the values in your report.
